I'm 68 years old and have been farming in Quzhou County my whole life. My family has about 6 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and I know this soil better than I know my own hands. At my age, I'm not going to gamble on new crops or fancy experiments. The wheat-maize double cropping system has fed my family for generations, and it works. The winter wheat I planted last October is already in the ground, and come early June I'll harvest it and immediately plant summer maize — there's no time to waste between crops, and every day counts for catching the summer heat. I've read enough and attended enough extension meetings over the years to know that throwing more fertilizer doesn't always mean more money, so I apply just what the crops need based on what I've observed. I'll use improved wheat seeds and hybrid maize because the yields are reliable and the seed quality is worth the cost. For the maize, I'll use no-tillage seeding right after the wheat harvest — it saves diesel, preserves soil moisture in this dry climate, and lets me plant faster. I'll keep one irrigation for the wheat in spring during green-up, one at jointing, one at heading, and one during grain filling. The maize will need water at sowing, jointing, and grain filling if the rains don't come. I don't spray chemicals more than necessary — twice for wheat, twice for maize, only when I see pests or disease pressure building. My neighbor's son tried vegetables last year and lost money; I stick to grain. It's mechanized, predictable, and at 68, my back can't handle the bending that vegetables require. My education taught me to keep records and calculate margins, and this plan gives me the steadiest income with the least risk.
